query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, service conditions that induce localized plastic deformation (e.g., low-temperature cyclic loading) lead to stress-driven, kinetic segregation of one or more minor atomic species to the grain boundaries. This segregation forms a thin, amorphous or complexion phase that is inherently brittle, causing a degradation of toughness even without the nucleation of conventional intermetallic particles.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with homogenously distributed elemental species and no pre-existing segregated or precipitated phases.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the HEA to controlled low-temperature cyclic loading that induces measurable plastic deformation while retaining the overall single-phase structure.
generation.conditions: Specifically, the alloy is aged under service conditions (low temperature and cyclic tensile or fatigue loading) that promote dislocation pile-ups. Comparison is made between samples exposed to these deformation cycles and an otherwise identically processed, undeformed control held at the same temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary segregation of one or more minor constituents leading to the formation of a thin, brittle interfacial complexion.
generation.mechanism: Under the imposed loading conditions, highly localized stresses near grain boundaries drive the diffusion of selected atoms to these interfaces. This creates compositionally heterogeneous grain boundaries that have reduced cohesive strength, eventually triggering a brittle failure mechanism rather than the ductile response observed in the baseline state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undeformed control, the cyclically loaded HEA samples will show a reduced fracture toughness along with microscopic evidence (using techniques such as atom probe tomography or high-resolution STEM-EDS) of enriched grain-boundary regions. No detectable bulk intermetallic precipitation is expected.
generation.baseline: An as-processed, undeformed single-phase high-entropy alloy that exhibits favorable strength–ductility combinations and high fracture toughness under standard service conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction applies to service conditions characterized by low temperature and cyclic (or fatigue) loading that induces plastic deformation, while maintaining the overall single-phase microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise identity and concentration of the segregating species are uncertain, as is the critical loading or temperature threshold required to initiate measurable grain-boundary segregation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of high-entropy alloy. One set is subjected to controlled low-temperature cyclic (fatigue) loading designed to induce plastic deformation without bulk phase changes; the other set is held as a static control at the same temperature. Post-treatment, perform mechanical fracture toughness tests and high-resolution microscopy (e.g., atom probe tomography, STEM-EDS) to assess grain-boundary composition.
measurements: Grain-boundary compositional profiling via atom probe tomography or STEM-EDS
Microstructural analysis to ensure the absence of conventional precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cyclically loaded samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness compared to the control, or if no evidence of enriched grain-boundary regions (brittle complexion) is observed, then the hypothesis that stress-induced grain-boundary segregation is responsible for brittleness in the single-phase HEA will be falsified.
